Meek
MEEK
adj. (from Hebrew anaw; Greek praus; characterized by strength under God's authority, humility without cowardice)
From Middle English meke, from Old Norse mjükr (soft, gentle, supple); cognate with Old English meoc. The KJV renders the Hebrew anaw (pl. anawim) and Greek praus as “meek.” The Hebrew root carries the sense of being bowed, afflicted, humbled before God; praus in Greek classical usage described a horse brought under its rider's authority — power controlled, not power absent. Meekness is therefore not weakness; it is strength submitted to the will of God.

Biblical Definition

Meekness in the biblical tradition names the disposition of the person who has been broken of self-assertion by God and now holds his own life and rights loosely before the divine will. Moses, the great leader of Israel, is described as “(Now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth.)” (Numbers 12:3), even as he confronted Pharaoh and led two million people through the wilderness — a portrait of meekness as courageous action without self-promotion. Jesus explicitly identifies Himself as “gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29) and calls His disciples to take His yoke, finding rest in that disposition. The third Beatitude promises earth-inheritance to the gentle/meek — not poverty of spirit alone but the character that waits on God for vindication rather than seizing it by force. Psalm 37 repeatedly directs the anawim to wait on the LORD while the wicked prosper, promising that they shall inherit the land and luxuriate in fullness of peace (37:11). The meek are those who do not retaliate, who endure injustice without self-vindication, who trust God to be Judge because they have stopped making themselves judge. This is the theological opposite of both self-pity (passive defeat) and self-assertion (pride defending its rights). The Reformed tradition, particularly in Owen and Sibbes, reads meekness as the fruit of mortification: the self-life has been weakened by grace enough that God's will can govern the spirit. Meekness is not natural temperament; it is the Spirit's work in the believer's soul.

Webster 1828 Definition

Meekness (Hebrew anaw; Greek praus) names the disposition of one who holds his life and rights loosely before God's sovereign will — strength submitted to divine authority, not weakness or timidity; the fruit of the Spirit mortifying self-assertion.

MEEK, adj. [Middle English meke; Old Norse mjükr, soft, supple.] Mild of temper; soft; gentle; not easily provoked or irritated; not self-asserting against the will of God; characterized by submission to the divine will without loss of courage or capacity for action. Webster 1828 distinguishes meekness from cowardice or servility; the meek man endures injuries without resentment because he has submitted his spirit to God's governance.

The Hebrew anaw (pl. anawim) describes those bowed or afflicted — those whose circumstances or chastisement has stripped self-reliance and left them cast on God alone. The Psalter celebrates the anawim as God's special objects of care (Pss. 22, 34, 37, 149). The anawim literature is the seedbed of the Beatitude tradition.

The Greek praus carried in classical usage the image of a tamed animal — specifically a war-horse whose power is now bridled and directed by its rider. This etymology recovers what the English “meek” easily loses: meekness is not the absence of power but power placed under authority. Christ's self-description as praus and tapeinos (Matthew 11:29) is not self-deprecation; it is the self-portrait of omnipotent deity who set aside His prerogatives to serve.

Reformed theology reads the third Beatitude — “Blessed are the gentle/meek, for they shall inherit the earth” — eschatologically: the meek do not seize the earth now by force but receive it as the gift of the coming kingdom, just as the anawim waited on the LORD in Psalm 37. Meekness is thus an eschatological virtue: it lives by promise, not by present possession.

The Puritan tradition (Owen, Sibbes, Baxter) treats meekness as the fruit of sanctification: as the Holy Spirit mortifies pride and self-will, the soul becomes increasingly capable of meekness toward God and man. It is not native temperament — the phlegmatic personality may appear meek while nursing pride within; the choleric believer, genuinely mortified, may display a deeper meekness than the outwardly mild-mannered unbeliever.

Key Scripture

Numbers 12:3 — "(Now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth.)"

Matthew 5:5 — "Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth."

Psalm 37:11 — "But the meek shall inherit the earth; and shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace."

Matthew 11:29 — "Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls."

Modern Corruption

Modern therapeutic culture has corrupted meekness in two directions: redefining it as doormat passivity (a psychological liability) or reclaiming it as “assertive gentleness” that validates the self while suppressing conflict — both evacuate the biblical sense of strength submitted to God.

expand to see more

The therapeutic register treats meekness as a psychological deficiency — the condition of the person who lacks appropriate self-assertion, suffers from low self-esteem, and requires healing into healthy boundaries and self-advocacy. In this reading, Jesus' command to be “gentle and humble in heart” becomes a symptom of dysfunction rather than a divine virtue. The secular psychological framework cannot recognize strength-under-authority because it has no category for a God whose authority is good, whose yoke is easy, and whose burden is light. The anawim are not victims awaiting therapy; they are warriors at rest in God.

A subtler corruption comes from within evangelical culture: “meekness” redefined as a communication style — speaking gently, maintaining a calm tone, avoiding confrontation — that has nothing to do with the disposition toward God the biblical term names. This produces leaders who are “meek” in public manner while harboring self-protection, reputation-management, and theological cowardice within. True meekness, as Moses demonstrates, is entirely compatible with confronting Pharaoh, breaking the golden-calf tablets in righteous anger, and interceding boldly for a rebellious nation. The meek man is not soft on God's enemies; he is submitted to God's verdict on them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Meekness as a biblical virtue flows from the anawim tradition of the Psalter (Pss. 22, 34, 37), the servant-portrait of Isaiah 42 and 53, and the Beatitude tradition of Matthew 5; it is fulfilled in Christ's self-emptying (Philippians 2:7–8) as the meek king who enters Jerusalem on a donkey.

expand to see more

Anawim (Psalm tradition) — the humble poor who throw themselves on God in the Psalter (Pss. 22, 34, 37, 149) are the OT seedbed of meekness; their prayer is the lament of those who have nothing left but God, and God meets them there.

Isaiah 53 (Servant of the LORD) — “He was oppressed, and He was afflicted, yet He opened not His mouth” (53:7); the Servant's meekness is not acquiescence to injustice but submission to the Father's redemptive will, the purest expression of the virtue.

Zechariah 9:9 (meek King) — “Your King is coming to you, gentle and mounted on a donkey”; the triumphal entry fulfills the promise of the anaw king who does not arrive on a war-horse but on the animal of peace, yet who will speak peace to the nations (9:10).

Matthew 5:5 (Beatitude promise) — “Blessed are the gentle/meek, for they shall inherit the earth” directly cites Psalm 37:11, connecting the eschatological inheritance of the anawim with kingdom citizenship; earth-inheritance is the consummated gift of the new creation.

Philippians 2:5–8 (Christ's kenosis) — Christ's self-emptying and becoming obedient even to death is the supreme act of meekness: omnipotence under the Father's authority, glory surrendered for the sake of the elect.

Usage

"Meekness is not passivity but the disposition of strength held under God's authority: Moses was meeker than all men and yet he confronted Pharaoh, led an army through a sea, and interceded boldly enough to turn God's wrath from Israel — the meek man does not shrink from hard tasks, he submits them to God."

"The Beatitude promise — “they shall inherit the earth” — is eschatological: the meek do not seize the earth now by self-assertion but receive it as the gift of the coming kingdom; this is why meekness endures injustice without vengeance, trusting the Judge who sees all."

"Pastors cultivating meekness in their congregations must name it correctly: not soft speech, not conflict-avoidance, not therapeutic “vulnerability” — but the Spirit-wrought disposition that has stopped making itself the final judge and has learned to wait on God's verdict."
